projects.description: Self-hosted agent runtime that runs long tasks using skills, memory, sandboxes, scheduled runs, and optional sub-agent delegation.
projects.canonical_data: threads, graph checkpoints, run events, scheduled tasks, sandbox workspace files, and Markdown memory facts
strengths: Four interfaces — terminal, web, HTTP gateway, and an embedded client — share one config, checkpointer, memory, and sandbox stack
Memory writes pass a deterministic scope and authority gate that fails closed, and facts stay readable Markdown files
Sandboxed execution spans host, Docker, Kubernetes, and remote VMs with capacity limits enforced across the deployment
weaknesses: Its documentation states that gateway administration is equivalent to running code on the host, so the admin role is not a containment boundary
Run events default to an in-memory backend, so run history and traces are lost on restart until reconfigured
Version 2.0 shares no code with version 1, so the operational track record is far shorter than the repository age implies
projects.why_it_matters: Shows what a long-horizon agent runtime looks like when memory, skills, sandboxes, and schedules ship as one operable system rather than a framework to assemble.

projects.name: CodeGraph
projects.description: Local code knowledge graph in SQLite that indexes symbols and call edges, syncs on file changes, and answers agent queries over MCP.
projects.canonical_data: a per-project SQLite graph of code symbols, call edges, and file hashes with a full-text index
strengths: Publishes per-language and per-framework extraction coverage measured on named public repositories rather than asserting accuracy
One SQLite graph serves nine coding agents plus a command line, an embeddable library, and a browser viewer
Marks uncertain edges as uncertain instead of presenting inferred relationships as fact
weaknesses: Telemetry ships enabled by default, with opt-out only after the installer prompt or an environment variable
Two continuous integration workflows, neither running tests, despite 236 test files in the repository
The schema keeps only current state, so no query can ask what the graph looked like before a change
projects.why_it_matters: Demonstrates that a code graph is more useful as shared local infrastructure many agents query than as a retrieval feature bundled inside one of them.

projects.name: GitNexus
projects.description: Code knowledge graph engine that indexes repositories and exposes graph, search, and impact queries to agents through MCP.
projects.canonical_data: a graph database of code symbols, relationships, embeddings, and cross-repository contract registries
strengths: Ships a real graph database with ad-hoc Cypher, hybrid keyword and vector search, and program-dependence queries
Cross-repository groups join microservice graphs through a provider and consumer contract registry for blast-radius analysis
Documents its own hosted-deploy weakness plainly, stating the bearer token is the only control on that deployment
weaknesses: The PolyForm Noncommercial license bars commercial use, and GitHub reports the repository as having no recognised license
The roadmap lists incremental indexing as unfinished while the command reference documents it as working
Twenty-two release candidates of a single patch version, three within about seventy minutes, indicate an unsettled release process
projects.why_it_matters: The most capable open code-graph engine for agents, and a clear case where a restrictive license and a vendor-run edition shape how a record must be classified.

projects.name: ECC
projects.description: A plugin that adds hooks, subagents, skills, and a local memory store to command-line coding agents.
projects.canonical_data: Markdown memory documents, YAML instincts, and a local SQLite session and install state store
strengths: Blocking hooks enforce discipline at tool-call time rather than relying on the model to follow written instructions
The memory design document states its own limits precisely, including lexical-only search and a named gap in its threat model
Eleven continuous integration workflows and validators lint every agent, skill, and hook definition in the repository
weaknesses: Only sixteen of 286 skills ship executable scripts; the large majority of the catalogue is documentation
The control plane that headlines version 2.0 is self-declared alpha, contradicting the project's battle-tested framing
Hook commands are long inline bootstrap blobs repeated across every entry, so a user cannot readily audit them before install
projects.why_it_matters: Shows that a coding-agent add-on can enforce process through blocking hooks and durable local memory rather than through prompt text alone.

projects.name: ruflo
projects.description: Command-line harness and MCP server giving coding agents durable memory, a coordination ledger, and scheduled background workers.
projects.canonical_data: vector-indexed agent memory and swarm and agent registries in local SQLite and record-file stores
strengths: The memory layer is genuinely built, with write-ahead SQLite, a vector index, encryption at rest, and expiry sweeps
Code comments repeatedly label the project's own stubs rather than reporting false success
Releases publish from tag-pinned checkouts with install smoke tests gating the registry write
weaknesses: The advertised swarm engine is not a dependency of the published package and is imported by nothing in the shipped command line
Coordination and spawn tools write records without dispatching any work, and several workflow step types are unimplemented
The project's own status and changelog documents trail the shipped version by twenty-eight and four minor releases
projects.why_it_matters: A widely adopted coding-agent harness whose durable memory substrate is real while its advertised swarm coordination remains a bookkeeping ledger.

projects.name: Orca
projects.description: Desktop app that runs several coding-agent command-line tools in parallel git worktrees with terminals, diffs, and mobile monitoring.
projects.canonical_data: workspace and worktree state plus orchestration runs, tasks, and inter-agent messages in a local database
strengths: Failure semantics are engineered rather than assumed, keeping an unverifiable verdict distinct from a confirmed exit
The terminal daemon outlives the application, so agent sessions survive a runtime restart or upgrade
Telemetry is enumerated field by field with three independent opt-outs, and the product has no account system
weaknesses: The inter-agent orchestration layer is gated behind an experimental setting and is absent from the project readme
The main runtime module is a single file of more than forty thousand lines against a repository-wide line-count ratchet
Open issues and pull requests both exceed two thousand, indicating triage is not keeping pace with the daily release cadence
projects.why_it_matters: Runs any terminal coding agent as a supervised process under one application, making parallel agent work reviewable rather than merely concurrent.

projects.name: Grok Bot
projects.description: Desktop and iOS product for creating named persistent agents that share one per-user cloud Linux computer with a browser, terminal, and filesystem.
projects.canonical_data: service-managed bot profiles, conversations, learned memory, skills, and routines, plus one per-user cloud computer holding workspace files, browser sessions, and command-line credentials
projects.current_repo_note: Covers the Grok Bot desktop and iOS product and its per-user cloud computer, not grok.com, Grok on X, or the xAI API. Authentication, administration, billing, and backend retention run through Cursor accounts while the service terms are xAI's; no first-party page reconciles the two.
strengths: Each bot is a durable named teammate with its own memory, skills, and routines rather than a session, and the documentation makes that the product's unit
Bots reach systems with no API by driving a real browser and terminal on a persistent virtual machine, handing control back to the person for passwords and challenges
Control surfaces are unusually complete for a new product, with per-action approvals, review rules where requiring approval wins over allowing, and a local-execution policy that asks by default
weaknesses: All of a user's bots share one computer with shared files and sign-in sessions, and the documentation states plainly that separate bots are not a security boundary
No administrator audit trail exists yet, leaving autonomous actions reviewable only through each bot's own conversation
Governance is split across two companies, with service terms from one and authentication, retention, and deletion following the other's
projects.why_it_matters: Establishes the persistent named agent with its own cloud computer, memory, routines, and peer handoffs as a shipping consumer product boundary distinct from the Grok assistant.

projects.name: OpenViking
projects.description: Self-hosted context store that keeps agent memories, resources, and skills under a virtual filesystem and serves them over an API, SDKs, and MCP.
projects.canonical_data: a virtual filesystem of memories, resources, and skills in tiered summaries over a local vector index and file store
projects.current_repo_note: The repository open-sources a subset of the capabilities described in the vendor's published paper; the commercial self-managed edition is activated by a license key whose code is not in this repository. The bundled agent module is a port of the separately published nanobot runtime.
strengths: Every query keeps the directory-browsing path that produced it, so a wrong result can be traced rather than attributed to an opaque similarity score
Client surfaces are deliberately permissive while the server stays copyleft, so an embedder can link the command line and TypeScript library without that reaching their own code
Runs offline in earnest, with local vector and file backends and an installer that detects and provisions a local model runtime
weaknesses: The Python library declares no license and so inherits the copyleft root, while its Go and TypeScript siblings are permissive
Every published benchmark figure is vendor-run on the vendor's own model and embeddings, at a version older than the current tree
The repository is less than eight months old and calls itself early stage, so its adoption implies more operational history than exists
projects.why_it_matters: Reframes agent memory as a browsable filesystem with tiered summaries rather than an opaque vector store, and already drops into a third-party runtime as an alternative to an established service.

projects.name: Supermemory
projects.description: Hosted memory and retrieval API for agents, with open client libraries, framework adapters, an MCP server, and applications in the repository.
projects.canonical_data: a hosted memory store behind the vendor's API, whose schema and engine are not in the repository
projects.current_repo_note: The repository holds client libraries, adapters, and applications. The memory engine is not present in it, and the self-hosted binary the documentation describes is distributed prebuilt from the vendor's site.
strengths: The framework adapter surface is unusually broad and genuinely permissive, spanning eight major frameworks plus a tool server
Memory lifecycle is specified as behavior rather than storage, naming supersession of stale facts and dated expiry
The vendor publishes an open harness for comparing memory systems head to head, which few in this space offer
weaknesses: The memory engine is absent from the repository while the documentation describes the binary as open source and links back to that same repository
Automated license detection reports a permissive license for a product whose engine is closed, so the signal is wrong without a human note
Every benchmark claim is self-reported against a harness the same vendor authors, with no readable pipeline to inspect
projects.why_it_matters: The most widely adopted agent memory API with genuinely open framework adapters, and a clean demonstration that a permissive root license is not a source-model conclusion.

projects.name: Onyx
projects.description: Self-hostable platform that indexes organizational sources through connectors and answers, searches, and runs agents over them in a chat interface.
projects.canonical_data: an index over source systems that remain canonical, held in a relational database and a search index the operator runs
projects.current_repo_note: The root license is a modified permissive license whose preamble places three enterprise directories under separate commercial terms; 229 of 3,347 backend Python files sit under the enterprise tree, and the project was formerly named Danswer.
strengths: The open-core boundary is drawn honestly and can be checked: the enterprise tree is governance, and the permissive deployment indexes, retrieves, and serves without it
Unusual breadth for a self-hostable product, with fifty-five connectors, deep research, tool actions, and desktop, mobile, command-line, and browser clients
Deployment is realistic, offering a light mode, air-gapped compose files in the tree, and an offline license upload path
weaknesses: Document-level permission sync and post-query filtering are enterprise-only, so the open edition cannot safely serve mixed-permission organizational data
The readme's license badge is a static image that misstates a repository with a real proprietary tier
Positioning has drifted toward general chat, and the light mode ships without a vector index at all
projects.why_it_matters: The most complete self-hostable knowledge-grounded product, and a reference for an open-core boundary that leaves the operational core genuinely usable.

projects.name: AFFiNE
projects.description: Local-first workspace for writing documents, building databases, and drawing on an unbounded canvas, with optional AI and server-based collaboration.
projects.canonical_data: a conflict-free replicated document store held locally on the device or synchronized through a server the operator runs
projects.current_repo_note: The root license places the entire server and native packages under separate enterprise terms, and self-hosted workspaces are capped at ten seats. The enterprise text also names a third license for community-edition parts that appears nowhere in the tree, so the license map cannot be closed from the repository alone.
strengths: The local-first path is real and permissively licensed, shipping local storage backends with their own indexers so an offline workspace never reaches the proprietary server
Its editor framework is a reusable permissive package, so the most valuable open component is consumable independently of the product
Self-hosted AI brings your own key across four providers, with per-workspace storage and a test step, rather than being hosted-only
weaknesses: The proprietary boundary is a whole tier rather than a feature overlay, with synchronization, search indexing, all AI, authentication, and payment in one licensed server
The repository asserts three licenses while shipping the text of two and no marker separating the editions
Self-hosted workspaces are capped at ten seats, and the team plan validates against the vendor unless a separate installable license is bought
projects.why_it_matters: The largest open local-first alternative to mainstream document and canvas tools, and the clearest case where a permissive client sits on an entirely proprietary server.

projects.name: oh-my-pi
projects.description: Terminal coding agent forked from Pi that adds a native execution core, language-server and debugger integration, and editor, remote-call, and shared-session surfaces.
projects.canonical_data: the local working tree, newline-delimited session logs, and local history and memory stores under the user's home directory
projects.current_repo_note: A hard fork of the published Pi record, sharing its early history and carrying the upstream author's copyright alongside its own; it stopped tracking upstream in January 2026. GitHub does not flag the repository as a fork.
strengths: Replaces shelling out with an embedded shell and in-process utilities, so common commands run without spawning processes and behave the same on Windows
The only reviewed coding agent that drives a real debugger, with adapters for three languages alongside language-server rename support
Attribution is unusually careful for a fork, with three-way copyright, per-component notices naming upstreams and local modifications, and generated third-party notices
weaknesses: Approval defaults to a permissive mode that auto-approves reads, writes, and shell execution, and no operating-system sandbox ships at all
The session-sharing relay defaults to a service the maintainer operates, whose source the documentation states is not published
More than two thousand open issues, a contribution policy that was gated and may be re-gated, and a four-toolchain build make independent verification expensive
projects.why_it_matters: The clearest case of a fork that outgrew its upstream, replacing a shell-out model with a native execution core and editor-grade language, debugger, and session surfaces.

projects.name: oh-my-claudecode
projects.description: Plugin and command-line tool for Claude Code that routes work to role-specific subagents and supervises fleets of terminal coding-agent workers in terminal panes.
projects.canonical_data: local project state under a dotted working directory, plus agent, skill, and command definitions kept as editable Markdown
projects.current_repo_note: An independent port of another author's project rather than a fork; it shares no history or code with it, and that project is not represented in the Atlas. The record is scored for the worker-supervision runtime it owns, not for capabilities the host agent supplies.
strengths: The worker-supervision layer is real machinery rather than prose, covering dispatch queues, mailboxes, pane readiness, merge coordination, and process identity locks
It supervises six competing vendors' coding-agent command-line tools as interchangeable workers
Test code exceeds implementation code, across more than seven hundred test files
weaknesses: The primary in-session surface runs nothing without the host agent and a paid subscription, so the record cannot claim the execution boundary it appears to describe
Thousands of build artifacts are committed, so the code that ships to the package registry is not reviewable against source without rebuilding
The marketplace manifest overstates the agent and skill counts present in the tree, and the near-empty issue queue reflects automated closing rather than triage
projects.why_it_matters: The most adopted worked example of an orchestrator that treats several competing vendors' coding agents as interchangeable supervised workers rather than as alternatives.

projects.name: Codewhale
projects.description: Terminal coding agent that runs against hosted or local model providers, with layered approval policy, operating-system sandboxing where available, and local browser and runtime interfaces.
projects.canonical_data: the local working tree, an append-only session journal, and Markdown memory files with a rebuildable full-text index under the user's home directory
projects.current_repo_note: Renamed from an earlier project of the same author and now provider-neutral; the project states it is unaffiliated with any model provider, though the repository name and a stale license copyright line both invite the opposite inference.
strengths: Authorization is specified before it is implemented, as nine ordered layers with a stated invariant that approval at one layer is never a universal bypass
The sandbox documentation refuses to claim capability it does not ship, naming which backends are wired and warning that source-only sandbox code is not evidence a command was restricted
Four coordinated local surfaces ship from one binary, including a web client that cannot be rebound off the loopback address
weaknesses: The license copyright still names the former project's contributors after the rename, so the file names an identity the project explicitly disclaims
Anonymous usage telemetry is enabled by default and posts to a first-party endpoint
Still before a first stable release, with active architectural churn and a self-reported gap in its third-party license notices
projects.why_it_matters: The clearest open example of a coding agent whose authorization order, sandbox availability, and telemetry contract are written down as falsifiable specifications rather than asserted as features.

projects.name: Reasonix
projects.description: Coding agent distributed as a single static binary, driven by a configuration file and plugin registry, with terminal, desktop, editor, and HTTP surfaces over one local engine.
projects.canonical_data: the local working tree, conversation transcripts, file-snapshot checkpoints, and a configuration file; the session catalogue is a rebuildable cache whose deletion never changes a conversation
projects.current_repo_note: The default branch is a ground-up rewrite on an orphan branch that shares no history with the original implementation, which remains abandoned on the branch a reader reaches by repository name. The project is a community effort and is not operated by the model provider its repository name carries.
strengths: Ships as a fully self-contained static binary cross-compiled to six targets, with nothing to install on the target machine beyond the binary
The architecture is written as a contract that leads the code, with an enforced acyclic dependency direction
Data ownership is reversible by design: checkpoints are file snapshots that never touch version history, and the session catalogue is an explicitly disposable cache
weaknesses: The published surface was rewritten from scratch on an orphan branch four months ago, and a reader arriving at the repository's named branch gets the abandoned implementation
More than sixteen hundred open issues stand against a codebase only three months old
Its lean-dependency principle means sandboxing and language-server support are reimplemented in the tree rather than delegated to hardened components
projects.why_it_matters: Shows that a full coding agent with plan mode, permissions, checkpoints, subagents, and editor and remote surfaces fits in one dependency-light static binary.

projects.name: Crush
projects.description: Terminal coding agent in Go with permission-gated tools, per-project session state, language-server and tool-server integration, and a local API for several clients.
projects.canonical_data: the working tree, a per-project session database, and a configuration file the user owns
projects.current_repo_note: Licensed under the Functional Source License, which bars competing commercial use and converts to a permissive licence two years after each release. An earlier period of the work carries a separate permissive grant from its original author.
strengths: Language-server operations are exposed as agent tools rather than as context alone, including rename and symbol replacement
One local backend serves several terminal clients over a socket, sharing session history, permission queue, and tool-server state
Ships as a single static binary packaged across eight operating-system families and every major package manager
weaknesses: The licence bars building a competing commercial product, a materially different position from every other published coding agent
Its own documentation notes that the project configuration is executed shell, so opening an untrusted repository is itself an execution decision
A stale generated annotation in the entry point advertises a permissive licence at a path that does not exist
projects.why_it_matters: The first source-available coding agent in the catalogue, and a self-contained runtime whose licence converts to permissive terms rather than staying restricted.

projects.name: Qwen Code
projects.description: Terminal coding agent forked from Gemini CLI, adding subagents, sandboxed execution, desktop and editor clients, language libraries, and messaging-platform channels.
projects.canonical_data: the working tree, project instructions, agent and skill definitions, and resumable local sessions
projects.current_repo_note: Forked from the published Gemini CLI record at version 0.8.2 and no longer syncing with it; hundreds of files still carry the upstream copyright alongside the fork's own. The vocabulary has no model-backend identifier for the maintainer's own models, so its native backend cannot be recorded.
strengths: The permission layer reasons about shell semantics and destructive commands rather than matching tool names, and is tested
Sandboxed execution through containers and hand-written platform profiles, in a role where most published records run on the host only
Reach no published coding agent matches, spanning a desktop app, three editor integrations, three language libraries, and messaging channels
weaknesses: Surface area outruns evidence, with several client packages thin relative to the core and two excluded from the main build
The headline installation path pipes a vendor-hosted script from a cloud bucket into a shell
Licence provenance needs care, with hundreds of core files still carrying the upstream author's copyright and three open licences across the tree
projects.why_it_matters: Shows a provider fork outgrowing its upstream, stopping its syncs and adding sandboxed execution, subagents, and a far wider client surface than the record it descends from.

projects.name: Continue
projects.description: Coding agent whose core runs as a separate process behind a command line, an editor extension, and a JetBrains plugin; released a final version and is no longer maintained.
projects.canonical_data: the working tree, a declarative agent configuration file, and command-line sessions under the user's home directory
projects.current_repo_note: The maintainers state the repository is no longer actively maintained and is read-only, following a final release that removed telemetry and authentication; the vendor was acquired. GitHub does not flag the repository as archived, so this status is editorial and rests on the maintainers' own statement.
strengths: One core packaged as a standalone process drives three clients, including the batch's only first-class JetBrains support
The permission design has an exclude level that hides a tool from the model entirely, with documented precedence resolution
Eighty-one model adapters, the widest provider surface reviewed, including four separate local-runtime paths
weaknesses: The product is finished: the repository is read-only, the final release is cut, and nothing further will be fixed
Headless mode's default policy allows shell execution and then allows every tool, so the strongest control is off where it matters most
The command line still contacts a vendor endpoint for version checks, against infrastructure nobody has committed to maintaining
projects.why_it_matters: A three-year open coding agent that removed its telemetry, authentication, and hosted coupling before freezing, leaving a self-contained final release.

projects.name: Roo Code
projects.description: Editor coding agent with user-definable modes, per-task checkpoints, and a compatibility layer letting its core run outside the editor; shut down in May 2026.
projects.canonical_data: the working tree, per-task checkpoint repositories, and user-defined mode definitions
projects.current_repo_note: Shut down in May 2026 and archived, with the extension delisted. Its own documentation names a community fork, Zoo Code, and its origin project as alternatives rather than declaring a successor, so the superseded status does not apply. That fork is excluded as packaging under the derivative rule, being identical to this record on every named field; a reader wanting a maintained agent in this lineage is served by the other published fork. It is the middle link between two published records, having forked from one and been forked into the other.
strengths: Per-task checkpoint repositories with navigation give genuine working-tree recovery, which its closest neighbours do not offer
A compatibility layer lets the same core run headless outside the editor, so one engine serves two front ends
Modes are first-class user-definable configuration with a published schema, giving reviewable role separation without a separate orchestration layer
weaknesses: Shut down in May 2026, with the repository archived and the extension delisted, so installing it now means building from source
Its command line auto-approves actions by default in interactive mode, inverting the safety posture the extension was known for
The live continuation is a community fork under different governance, so the reviewed privacy commitments no longer bind whoever ships the code
projects.why_it_matters: The most widely installed editor coding agent to shut down mid-flight, and the middle link in a fork chain whose other two records the Atlas publishes.

projects.name: Vane
projects.description: Self-hosted web application that answers a question by running a bounded search-and-scrape loop over a local search engine and returning a cited answer.
projects.canonical_data: chat messages and the response blocks recorded against them in a local database
projects.current_repo_note: Renamed from Perplexica within the same history, so it stays one record with a note. Development has been quiet: the most recent code change predates this review by several months, and two features the readme advertises are absent from the source.
strengths: The research step is an explicit bounded tool loop with its own registry and a deliberate finish action, rather than a fixed retrieval pipeline
The plan is a first-class part of the interface, streamed to the reader as reasoning before any other tool runs
Fully self-operable from one container, with four of its eight model providers running locally
weaknesses: No test suite and no continuous integration beyond building a container image
Search and scrape failures are logged and dropped inside the retrieval layer, so a run can quietly degrade to a thin evidence set
Effectively dormant, with no code change for several months and advertised search providers missing from the source
projects.why_it_matters: The only fully self-hostable cited-answer engine reviewed whose research step is an inspectable tool loop rather than a fixed retrieval pipeline.

projects.name: dexter
projects.description: Terminal agent that answers financial research questions by planning tool calls across a market-data service, filings, and web search, then writing a sourced summary.
projects.canonical_data: tool-call logs written per run, a local memory database, and user-editable instruction files
projects.current_repo_note: No licence file has ever existed in this repository and the package manifest declares none; a single readme sentence claims permissive terms, which is the only artifact granting anything. Two memory modules credit a third-party project in comments without a corresponding licence file.
strengths: A permission engine parses shell commands and fails closed to asking, with dedicated tests behind it
Domain depth is implemented rather than prompted, spanning statements, filings, insider trades, institutional holdings, and screening
Every tool call is durably recorded with arguments, raw result, and summary, so a run can be reconstructed afterwards
weaknesses: No licence file has ever existed and the manifest declares none, so redistribution terms rest on one readme sentence
Headline capabilities the readme advertises are prompt behaviour rather than machinery; the loop is a plain iteration with a fixed cap
All financial data flows through a single hard-coded commercial endpoint owned by the maintainer, with no alternative path
projects.why_it_matters: Shows what a vertical research agent looks like when domain tools rather than the prompt carry the specialisation, and how far a permission model reaches without a sandbox.

projects.name: deepagents
projects.description: Python library that assembles a preconfigured agent with a filesystem, subagent delegation, skills, and context management on top of an existing agent loop.
projects.canonical_data: application-defined agent state, plus files held in a pluggable storage backend the integrator chooses
projects.current_repo_note: Its own architecture document states it is an opinionated harness over the vendor's existing agent constructor and introduces no new runtime; the vendor's framework and graph runtime are published separately. The companion library in another language is the same product and is not recorded separately. Benchmark corpora vendored under the evaluation package carry their own permissive notices from their upstream projects.
strengths: It owns substantial machinery of its own, including a storage protocol with eight implementations and per-model harness profiles
Correctness infrastructure is unusually strong for a pre-1.0 library, with warnings treated as errors and three external benchmarks run in continuous integration
Approval is a construction-time parameter that compiles down to runtime interrupts, rather than an integration exercise
weaknesses: It is structurally inseparable from the framework beneath it, which is published separately, and its own documents say it adds no new runtime
The vendor's hosted tracing service is a required dependency of the core package and its sandbox is a first-class backend
It ships before a first stable release, with an active deprecation on its main entry point and an alpha sub-runtime its own documentation excludes from production
projects.why_it_matters: The clearest example of a harness layer that adds enough of its own machinery to be a separate build target rather than a convenience wrapper over the framework beneath it.

projects.name: Skyvern
projects.description: Browser-workflow agent that plans and executes tasks on websites through a driven browser and vision models, with a workflow builder, self-hosted server, libraries, and a managed cloud.
projects.canonical_data: tasks, workflow definitions and runs, steps and actions, screenshots and recordings, credentials, and extracted data in a database the operator runs plus artifact storage
projects.current_repo_note: Every file in the repository is copyleft; the proprietary parts — anti-bot and captcha solving, enterprise gating, billing, and cloud browser vendors — live outside it and plug in by overriding base classes whose open implementations return nothing. A workflow sync mirrors merged changes into a private cloud repository.
strengths: A budgeted, retrying step loop with a failure classifier, and a second-generation tool-calling engine with stall detection
One codebase covers a command line, an embedded library, a self-hosted server with a workflow builder, container orchestration, and a cloud
Broad model backends including local and compatible endpoints, plus a tool server and workflow-automation integrations
weaknesses: The advertised anti-bot and captcha solving are cloud-only overrides of open stubs that return nothing
Telemetry is on by default, and the workflow code block executes user Python in the server process behind an allowlist rather than a sandbox
Package releases trail the repository's tags, and the quick-install path has shipped broken releases
projects.why_it_matters: The most complete self-hostable browser agent with a workflow builder and credential handling, and a clear demonstration of where an open core stops and the vendor cloud begins.

projects.name: CowAgent
projects.description: Self-hosted personal agent runtime that plans and runs tool calls over per-agent workspaces holding memory, knowledge, skills, and schedules, reachable from a web console, terminal, desktop app, and messaging channels.
projects.canonical_data: per-agent workspaces of identity, memory, knowledge, and skill files plus a scheduler store, alongside a local database of sessions, messages, runs, and memory chunks
projects.current_repo_note: Renamed from chatgpt-on-wechat within the same history, so it stays one record. The rename changed nothing operational; the change that earns this role is the 2.0 agent core released ten weeks earlier, before which the project was a messaging bridge. The container image, compose file, and package metadata still carry the former name.
strengths: Standing named agents are the runtime's unit, each with its own workspace, memory, skills, sessions, scheduler, and channel bindings, with delegation between them recorded as parent and child runs
Memory is a real three-tier system with full-text and vector search in one local database and a scheduled distillation pass, all held in readable Markdown
The broadest coverage of Chinese messaging platforms of any reviewed runtime, alongside the Western ones
weaknesses: The permission model checks tool arguments rather than sandboxing, and defaults to full access on existing installations
Continuous integration runs no general test suite, so the substantial test tree is only as good as the maintainer's local runs
Development is effectively single-maintainer, and the container image and package metadata still carry the pre-rename identity
projects.why_it_matters: Shows a messaging-bot repository turning into a multi-agent personal runtime while keeping its channel reach, with peer delegation recorded as durable runs rather than ephemeral subagents.

projects.name: nanobot
projects.description: Self-hosted personal agent runtime with version-controlled Markdown memory, scheduled automations, skills, subagents, and many chat channels, exposed through a terminal, web console, Python library, and compatible API.
projects.canonical_data: an agent workspace of identity, user, and memory files, an append-only history log, heartbeat and scheduled jobs, and skills under version control, plus session files kept outside it
projects.current_repo_note: The discovery sweep read 'framework' from the tagline, but the readme calls it a self-hosted personal agent runtime two sections later and the code agrees. It is the upstream of the agent module vendored into the published OpenViking record, which ports it at an early version. The package still classifies itself as alpha.
strengths: Memory is layered and auditable: an append-only history, a consolidator, a scheduled distillation pass, and version-control history of every durable-file change
The same runtime is reachable as a command line, a web console, a compatible model endpoint, and a Python library, so it embeds without forking, which a published memory record already did
Interrupted turns recover from checkpoints without replaying tool calls that had side effects
weaknesses: The lightweight claim describes a small core, not the package, whose channel code alone is several times larger
Process isolation has one backend and is Linux-only; other platforms get application-level guards the code says are not a sandbox
Control governs who may talk to the agent rather than what it may run; there is no approval step before a tool executes
projects.why_it_matters: The most widely adopted open runtime of its shape that is also a library, and the upstream of the agent bundled into a published memory system.

projects.name: screenpipe
projects.description: Local screen and audio recorder that stores recognised text, transcripts, and frame metadata in a local database and exposes them to agents over an HTTP API and a tool server.
projects.canonical_data: a local database of recognised text, transcripts, and frame and audio metadata alongside local video and audio files
projects.current_repo_note: Relicensed in June 2026 from a permissive licence to a custom commercial licence covering the whole tree, which permits personal, non-profit, and short evaluation use and requires a paid licence for commercial use; earlier permissive releases remain available under their original terms. Several library manifests still declare an enterprise identifier with no matching licence file, which the library readme says is superseded by the root licence. Release builds check for a paid plan.
strengths: The only ambient-capture system reviewed with an agent-facing API and tool-server endpoint, so what was seen and heard is retrievable by software rather than only by a person
Explicit retention auto-deletion, raw query, and export controls over a database the user holds
Broad continuous integration across three platforms with end-to-end, chaos, and evaluation suites, and near-daily releases
weaknesses: Since June 2026 no part of the tree is under an open licence, and the licence claims ownership of contributors' modifications
Product analytics and crash reporting are on by default in the desktop app despite the claim that everything is local
Release builds are subscription-gated, so the free path is building from a fast-moving multi-toolchain tree
projects.why_it_matters: Shows the ambient-capture category migrating from open hobby projects to a venture-backed source-available product with an agent interface.

projects.name: Hindsight
projects.description: Self-hosted memory server that extracts facts from what an agent retains, consolidates them into evidence-backed observations and standing mental models, and serves recall and reflection over an API, libraries, and a tool server.
projects.canonical_data: a relational database with vector extensions, or an embedded equivalent, holding facts, entities, observations, and mental models scoped to memory banks
projects.current_repo_note: Independently confirmed as a swappable memory backend in the published oh-my-pi record, whose client posts to this server's bank-scoped endpoints; that is the same evidence shape that settled OpenViking. The drop-in model-client wrapper defaults to the vendor's hosted endpoint unless configured otherwise.
strengths: Consolidation produces beliefs with quoted evidence and proof counts instead of overwriting facts
Ships a real service surface of four client languages, a command line, and a per-bank tool-server endpoint that a third-party coding agent already uses as a pluggable backend
Runs offline in earnest, with an embedded database and local embedding and reranking models
weaknesses: Every published accuracy figure is vendor-run and the accompanying paper is the vendor's own
The drop-in model-client wrapper points at the vendor's cloud unless told otherwise
The API and configuration surface is very large for a pre-1.0 release
projects.why_it_matters: The strongest current case that agent memory should consolidate into standing, evidence-backed beliefs rather than a searchable pile of extracted facts, already wired into an independent runtime.

projects.name: CAMEL
projects.description: Python framework for building societies of role-playing and workforce agents, with a coordinator that decomposes tasks, assigns workers, and recovers from failures.
projects.canonical_data: application-defined agent memory and workforce task state
projects.current_repo_note: Paper-associated and maintained by a research collective, but with a real release train, a large test suite, and continuous integration, so it passes the test that excluded paper harnesses. Framework-primary is a defensible alternative reading; the flagship module, name, and description are the multi-agent society. A separate commercial product is built on it by the same organisation.
strengths: A full orchestration runtime with pause, snapshot, and resume rather than a prompt pattern
Failure handling that creates new workers at runtime is implemented and tested
Provider and sandbox breadth without any vendor lock, including local runtimes and container execution
weaknesses: The release train stalled at pre-release alphas for five months while commits continued
Two files of over six thousand lines each hold the orchestrator and the chat agent, making audit costly
Research-collective governance with a separate commercial product sitting on top
projects.why_it_matters: The oldest surviving role-playing multi-agent framework, now carrying a production-style workforce orchestrator alongside its research heritage.

projects.name: Open Design
projects.description: Desktop and command-line workspace that runs the user's installed coding-agent tool against design skills, design-system files, and templates to produce prototypes, decks, images, and video, with a sandboxed preview and export.
projects.canonical_data: project folders of generated output and assets plus a local database of projects, conversations, messages, runs, and agent sessions
projects.current_repo_note: Four months old at review with the highest adoption in the queue. Its daemon spawns and supervises the host agents itself, so the reserved add-on question does not apply. The licence file is a silently modified Apache text: one clause in the redistribution section is shortened and the warranty section is retitled; the platform still detects the standard licence. Packaged beta builds bundle a closed third-party command-line tool.
strengths: The adapter layer is a data contract, so many vendors' agent tools are driven by one generic engine
A tool-loop guard and run-failure classification give the wrapper its own failure semantics instead of streaming a stuck agent forever
Test volume in the daemon exceeds its implementation, and browser suites run on every change
weaknesses: The licence text is a silently modified Apache licence, and packaged beta builds bundle an unlicensed third-party tool
A single composition file of nearly seventeen thousand lines holds the process-spawn path alongside everything else
A safety-telemetry channel that the analytics toggle cannot disable, and a readme that leads with a paid model service
projects.why_it_matters: The most adopted example of a workflow layer that owns its own daemon, persistence, and process supervision around whichever coding agent the user already runs.

projects.name: AionUi
projects.description: Desktop and web application with a bundled agent engine that runs file, document, web, and scheduled tasks, and supervises third-party coding-agent tools and agent teams over the Agent Client Protocol.
projects.canonical_data: conversations, sessions, assistants, teams, and scheduled jobs in local databases owned by the desktop app and its backend, plus Markdown assistant and skill definitions
projects.current_repo_note: The operational core is a first-party backend fetched as a binary from a second repository at packaging time, and the bundled engine is a third first-party repository; under ADR 020 the three are one product. The backend's package manifest declares a permissive licence that differs from its licence file. Reviewing this repository alone reviews the shell.
strengths: Team coordination is real machinery: a scheduler, mailbox, work coordinator, and crash recovery rather than prose
It works without any third-party tool because a first-party engine is bundled
A headless server and standalone web runtime are documented alongside the desktop build
weaknesses: The operational core is a binary fetched from a second repository at packaging time
The backend's package manifest declares a different licence from its licence file
Design documents and much of the changelog rationale are in one language only, and partner promotions precede the product description in the readme
projects.why_it_matters: A desktop agent product where one runtime hosts a bundled engine and competing vendors' tools as interchangeable protocol workers, including in supervised teams.

projects.name: Jan
projects.description: Desktop chat application that runs local models through bundled engines or cloud providers, with projects, assistants, file context, tool servers, and a local compatible API.
projects.canonical_data: threads as line-delimited files, assistants and settings as structured files, and model files in a user-relocatable local folder, plus a local vector index for project files
projects.current_repo_note: The licence file is a short notice naming the Apache licence rather than its text, the platform detects no licence, and several package manifests still declare the copyleft licence the project used before 2025 while others declare a permissive one; the readme and the notice agree on the current licence. Its inference engine is the separately published llama.cpp record, which names this product as a downstream boundary. A terminal coding agent in the same repository is distributed separately in preview and is not part of this record.
strengths: Everything is a readable local file, with threads, assistants, and model manifests in a relocatable data folder
Local engines and cloud providers share one project and assistant model, re-exposed through a local compatible server
Tool-server support includes dynamic registration and standards-based authorisation with tokens kept in a separate owner-only file
weaknesses: The licence file is a notice rather than the licence text, the platform reports none, and manifests disagree with each other
The Apple-silicon engine path is documented as experimental without embeddings
No stable release in six weeks against daily commits, with agent surfaces moving faster than the documentation that gates them
projects.why_it_matters: The reference open desktop counterpart to hosted chat assistants, holding conversations, projects, and models on the user's own disk with no server to operate.

projects.name: mini-SWE-agent
projects.description: Small Python coding agent whose only tool is the shell, run interactively from a terminal with confirmation before each command or as a library, against a local shell, a container, or a remote sandbox.
projects.canonical_data: the working tree of the local or container environment, plus a trajectory file rewritten after every step
projects.current_repo_note: Declared successor to SWE-agent in that project's readme, and the maintainers' own boundary statement lives in this project's documentation: prefer this for a simple local tool and stable sandboxing, and the predecessor for custom tools and rich configuration. The second major version changed the trajectory format with a migration guide. The package still carries an alpha classifier at version 2.4.
strengths: The loop is roughly a hundred lines and tested, so what runs is what you read
Confirmation is the interactive default, rejections are fed back to the model as steering, and a three-mode switch is documented
One design runs unchanged on the host, containers, and remote sandboxes because each action is an independent process
weaknesses: The command-line default environment is the host with no isolation, and the sandbox backends are opt-in or marked experimental
The shell is the only tool, so file edits are model-issued stream edits and here-documents with no structured edit primitive
The package still declares alpha status at version 2.4, and the last release is six weeks old
projects.why_it_matters: The maintainers of SWE-agent replaced their own tool-rich scaffold with a shell-only loop and published the boundary between the two, making it the reference for how little harness a coding agent needs.

projects.name: SWE-agent
projects.description: Configurable coding agent that resolves repository issues in a container through a tested library loop and tool bundles, kept for research reproducibility after its authors moved development to a simpler successor.
projects.canonical_data: per-run trajectory files and the container working tree
projects.current_repo_note: Its readme states that mini-SWE-agent has superseded it and recommends the successor going forward, which ADR 016 records now that the successor is published. It passes the research-artifact test that excluded other paper projects: the loop is in a tested library with continuous integration. No package has been distributed since a placeholder in 2024, and the last release is from May 2025.
strengths: The loop and tools live in a tested library with continuous-integration coverage, not a demo
Trajectories are first-class and replayable, with an inspector and a replay runner
Execution is in a container by default
weaknesses: Its own maintainers recommend against it in favour of the successor
No distributed package exists beyond a 2024 placeholder, and there has been no release since May 2025
No action approval exists in the primary run path; the person is either the model or absent
projects.why_it_matters: The reference scaffold that defined the agent-computer-interface pattern, now kept for reproducibility while its authors moved on.

projects.name: agenticSeek
projects.description: Self-hosted multi-agent assistant that routes a request to a coding, file, browser, or planning agent, runs that agent's tool loop against a local model, and answers through a terminal or web interface.
projects.canonical_data: per-agent conversation sessions saved as structured files under the runtime directory, plus files the agents write inside the configured workspace
projects.current_repo_note: Covers two of the role's four surfaces: files and the web, but not applications or scheduled work; its tool-server agent is disabled as non-functional and no scheduler exists. It passes the operational test that excluded paper projects, with the loop in a library behind a real test suite, but no continuous integration runs those tests and no release has ever been cut.
strengths: The browser agent is a genuine navigation loop with form filling, stuck detection, and an explicit exit action
Workspace confinement and loopback-only publishing were added deliberately, with tests behind the safe-mode fix
Local models are the primary path and every hosted key is optional
weaknesses: No continuous integration and no release has ever been cut, so the test suite is only as good as the maintainer's machine
Command execution runs unconfirmed by default, safe mode is a word blocklist, and the browser prompt tells the model never to ask the user
Two of the role's four surfaces are absent, and the tool-server agent is disabled as non-functional
projects.why_it_matters: The most-adopted attempt at a fully local general work agent, showing how far router-plus-planner delegation reaches on consumer hardware before connectors and scheduling exist.

projects.name: DocsGPT
projects.description: Self-hostable platform that ingests documents, web sources, connectors, and audio into a searchable knowledge base and answers questions and runs configurable agents over it, exposing those agents through widgets, a compatible API, and a tool server.
projects.canonical_data: uploaded and connected sources chunked into a vector store the operator selects, with users, agents, conversations, and memory-tool files in a relational database
projects.current_repo_note: Not open core: the governance features the vendor's enterprise tier lists — role management, single sign-on with provisioning, teams, and connectors — are all in the permissive tree, and the paid tiers are hosting and support. The recommended quick-start path routes inference through the vendor's public endpoint with a shared key, and version checks contact the vendor unless disabled.
strengths: The governance features a competitor sells as enterprise — role management, single sign-on with provisioning, and teams — are in the permissive tree and documented
Agents are first-class integration surfaces: any compatible client or tool-server host can call a configured agent
A real correctness gate, with thousands of tests run on every push and coverage reported
weaknesses: The default quick-start routes all inference through the vendor's public endpoint with a shared key
Version checks contact the vendor by default
The memory tool and lifecycle are thin, with path-keyed overwrite and no consolidation or temporal handling, and graph retrieval is gated to one store
projects.why_it_matters: A complete permissively licensed knowledge platform whose enterprise governance is not withheld, and which turns each knowledge agent into an endpoint other software can call.

projects.name: MemOS
projects.description: Self-hostable memory service and Python library that extracts memories from conversations and files into graph and vector stores organised as per-user memory cubes, serves add, search, and feedback over an API and a tool server, and ships local plugins for three agent runtimes.
projects.canonical_data: per-user memory cubes of extracted memory items held in a graph database and a vector store the operator runs, with users and cubes in a relational store; the agent plugins keep a local file database
projects.current_repo_note: Paper-associated but maintained by a company with a hosted product, a release roughly every one to two weeks, and a multi-platform continuous-integration matrix, so it passes the test that excluded paper harnesses. No published runtime it targets names it as a backend; its integrations run one way from its own adapters, unlike Hindsight and OpenViking, which were confirmed from the runtime side. Plugin directories declare a permissive licence in their manifests with no licence file, and a vendored third-party desktop app carries its own.
strengths: A real service surface of an API, a tool server, a library, and a command line, with a continuous-integration matrix that builds and installs the package on four platforms
Memory cubes give explicit isolation and sharing boundaries across users and agents rather than a single flat store
The local plugin brings the same core to three agent runtimes on-device with a file database and hybrid recall
weaknesses: No runtime it targets names it as a backend; one of them lists eight other memory services and not this one
Licence metadata is inconsistent, with permissive manifests beside no licence file and a badge that links to a different licence text
Defaults are not sovereign: a hosted model provider for every model, telemetry on in the plugin, and every accuracy figure vendor-run
projects.why_it_matters: The most complete open memory service organised around explicit per-user, per-agent memory cubes, shipping both a self-hosted server and on-device plugins, even though the runtimes it targets have not yet reciprocated.

projects.name: MagenticLite
projects.description: Locally installed browser and filesystem agent that runs its browser inside a virtual-machine sandbox and pairs a small orchestrator model with a separate vision model for browser actions.
projects.canonical_data: sessions, runs, messages, settings, and trusted-folder grants in a local database, plus per-run screenshots and the folders the user has mounted
projects.current_repo_note: Renamed and rewritten within one repository and one package, so it stays one record; the rewrite replaced most of the tree and removed the collaborative planning feature the earlier version was known for. Its dependency on the vendor's superseded agent framework has been severed entirely: the current package manifest names none of it. The maintainer describes it as a research prototype and advises against production use, and the package still declares an alpha classifier.
strengths: It runs the browser inside a virtual machine by default rather than a container or the bare host, the strongest isolation boundary of any browser agent reviewed

Human control is machinery rather than prompting: a large command policy with deny patterns, approval required for anything untrusted as the shipped default, an explicit grant table for folders, mid-run steering, and browser takeover, each with tests behind it
It is engineered to run on small models, with a documented end-to-end self-hosting path that makes a fully operator-controlled deployment achievable rather than theoretical
weaknesses: The rewrite deleted the collaborative planning feature the project was known for, which its own public description still advertises
The maintainer explicitly advises against commercial or real-world use and the package still declares alpha status after sixteen releases

Provider breadth is thin and momentum has stalled: two model clients, no tool-server support, a browser role that accepts only two model variants, and six weeks with no human merge while dependency updates queue
projects.why_it_matters: The only browser agent reviewed that ships as an installed local application running its browser inside a virtual machine, and the clearest demonstration that a capable agent loop can be built for small self-hostable models rather than frontier ones.

projects.name: TaskWeaver
projects.description: Archived code-first agent that answers data-analysis requests by planning, generating, and verifying Python, then executing it in a stateful kernel that preserves in-memory data across turns.
projects.canonical_data: per-session workspace directories with conversation files, an execution working directory, distilled experience files, and plugin definitions the user authors
projects.current_repo_note: Archived by its maintainer with no notice on the readme or the still-live documentation site, so both surfaces still read as an active project. It was never published to a package index; the only install paths are a clone or a version-control URL against one of two tags, against a declared version far beyond them.
strengths: Code verification is real machinery rather than a prompt, walking the syntax tree with configurable allow and block lists and an explicit dangerous-builtins list, feeding a bounded revise-and-retry loop

Stateful execution is the design centre: the kernel keeps in-memory tables alive across turns, so multi-step analysis composes instead of restarting, which is the specific thing query-generating agents cannot do
Unusually broad provider coverage for its era, spanning five vendors plus local runtimes, with container execution by default and a published executor image
weaknesses: The repository is archived with no notice on the readme or the live documentation site, so both still read as active
It was never published to a package index, so it cannot be a dependency and the only install paths are a clone or a version-control URL
No approval step exists before generated code runs, which its own contribution wish-list asks for, and there is no tool-server support
projects.why_it_matters: The clearest worked example of a data agent built on generated Python over live in-memory state rather than on generated queries, with syntax-tree verification of that code before it runs.

projects.name: Omnigent
projects.description: Meta-harness that runs a declaratively defined agent on any of a dozen vendors' coding-agent harnesses, with its own policy engine, operating-system sandboxes, and a self-hosted server reachable from terminal, browser, desktop, and phone.
projects.canonical_data: sessions, conversations, agent and policy definitions, projects, files, and scheduled tasks in a self-hosted database the operator chooses, plus per-session working trees on the host
projects.current_repo_note: Published under a neutral organisation but first-party to a named company, which holds the copyright and is the package author. A framework reading is genuinely arguable and the package's own summary takes it; the orchestrator reading rests on the routing relay that interposes on a harness's own subagent spawn and on mixing several vendors' agents in one session. Its third-party notice attributes two copyleft dependencies, neither of which is vendored into the tree.
strengths: The harness abstraction is real and symmetric, with paired executor modules for about a dozen competing vendors' agents, a capability matrix, and a contribution-gating bench that checks each against observed behaviour

Control is engineered as a first-class layer rather than prompt text: stacked server, agent, and session policies evaluated in a deliberately non-Turing-complete expression language, with spend caps and credentials brokered away from the agent

Correctness infrastructure is unusual for a three-month-old project, with a sharded test matrix, separate runs against two database engines, and a parity job that builds a sidecar to check a wrapped vendor tool
weaknesses: It is pre-release and says so, while more than a thousand open issues have accumulated in under three months
The subagent routing gate is advisory by design: any transport failure, timeout, or unparseable verdict silently allows the spawn, so the routing policy is not a boundary a reader can rely on
Telemetry is enabled by default and fetches its own remote configuration from a vendor endpoint, so a fully offline install requires opting out before first run
projects.why_it_matters: The most complete attempt so far to make competing vendors' coding agents interchangeable executors behind one declarative agent file, one policy layer, and one sandbox.

projects.name: Open SWE
projects.description: Self-hosted system that takes code-change and code-review tasks from a dashboard, a code host, chat, or a schedule, works in a per-thread sandbox, and delivers pull requests.
projects.canonical_data: durable threads and checkpoints bound to persistent sandboxes, plus pull requests, review findings, learned review preferences, skills, and automation definitions
projects.current_repo_note: The repository is permissively licensed, but the agent server it pins for production self-hosting is licensed on restricted terms and gated on a licence key, so the permissive badge covers the graphs and not the runtime that serves them. That runtime's licence has no identifier in the vocabulary and is recorded under the general commercial reference. The project was repositioned in September 2026 beyond the framing of its original announcement, which is a scope change on one record rather than supersession.
strengths: It owns the whole delivery loop rather than the agent turn, with five distinct graphs, dozens of purpose-built tools, and a reviewer evaluated in continuous integration against golden comments mined from five real open-source repositories

Authorisation and containment are product features rather than deployment advice, with organisation and repository allowlists checked against the actor, approval before workflow-file pushes, and read-only review and chat graphs
Failure semantics are stated and enforced: a store outage raises rather than reading as empty, and an unreachable sandbox fails the run rather than being silently replaced and losing uncommitted work
weaknesses: Production self-hosting is not fully open, because the agent server it pins is licensed on restricted terms and gated on a licence key

The vendor's own platform is the default for both sandboxing and tracing, and its key appears among the standalone deployment's required settings, so the lowest-friction path routes work and traces through that service
Models are a closed list in the dashboard with no compatible endpoint or local runtime, so a deployer who self-hosts the infrastructure still cannot self-host the model
projects.why_it_matters: The clearest worked example of a coding agent packaged as deployable infrastructure, with triggers, sandboxes, review, and delivery, rather than as a library an integrator has to assemble.

projects.name: Swarms
projects.description: Python framework whose director agent parses typed orders and dispatches them to named worker agents, with dozens of prebuilt coordination structures and a command-line interface.
projects.canonical_data: application-defined agent conversations and swarm task state
projects.current_repo_note: Its dispatch was verified by running the published package offline against stub workers with no network, so the failure recorded against another orchestrator, whose advertised engine was absent from its shipped package, does not apply here. The overstatement is in the marketing rather than the machinery: the readme promises an availability guarantee and enterprise high-availability for a library whose own manifest declares beta status, and its citation file names a version many majors behind what ships.
strengths: The hierarchical dispatch is typed machinery in the shipped package rather than a prompt pattern, gated on a schema parsed from the director's tool call that raises rather than degrading to text
Dozens of structures cover genuinely distinct coordination shapes, each with a matching test module
Recent maintenance is corrective rather than promotional, reading as a defect-fix train through the coordination structures themselves
weaknesses: The test gate is nominal: not one passing run in the last thirty, every one killed at the workflow's timeout, so no change to the coordination structures has been mechanically verified
Telemetry is on by default and carries task text, model output, and serialised conversation state to a vendor endpoint behind a single environment variable
No approval, interrupt, or gating primitive exists anywhere in the coordination structures, and published release notes stopped nine major versions ago
projects.why_it_matters: The most heavily forked general multi-agent orchestrator whose dispatch really is implemented in the shipped package, wrapped in enterprise claims its own release metadata contradicts.

projects.name: emdash
projects.description: Desktop application that runs several third-party coding-agent command lines in parallel, each in its own working tree, with issue-tracker intake, diff review, pull-request handling, scheduled automations, and remote workspaces.
projects.canonical_data: a working tree per task plus a local database of workspaces, conversations, automation deployments, and pull-request state
projects.current_repo_note: The sweep proposed a coding-agent role, but no model client exists anywhere in the tree: it drives thirty-eight vendors' tools over one protocol contract. It is not the terminal-manager shape that excluded two earlier candidates, because its persisted schema carries workspaces, conversations, automation deployments, and pull-request state rather than a flat list of sessions, and it ships a scheduling runtime and a remote daemon of its own. Nothing hosts it, so the reserved add-on question is not reached.
strengths: The test job is a required gate on every change and provisions native database and terminal builds specifically so the migration and terminal specs actually execute rather than being skipped
Concurrency is designed rather than asserted, with seven of its own decision records settling workspace ownership, a single-writer registry, best-effort cancellation, and reconciled deletion
One generic protocol and plugin contract drives thirty-eight agent tools and reaches remote machines through a separately versioned daemon, so the reach does not come from per-vendor special cases
weaknesses: It executes nothing agentic itself, so its usefulness is entirely contingent on other vendors' tools and their protocol support
Only two of the thirty-eight adapters ship a bundled protocol asset; the rest require the user to have installed and authenticated the vendor's own tool
Telemetry is enabled by default in code, and nearly two hundred issues are open against a product that reached its first stable version weeks ago
projects.why_it_matters: The most adopted attempt to make parallel, isolated coding-agent runs a reviewable delivery process, and the only reviewed system driving many vendors' agents through one protocol contract instead of per-vendor glue.

projects.name: stagewise
projects.description: Desktop browser with a built-in coding agent that reads the open tab's console and page structure, edits the connected codebase, and can also drive external agents over a client protocol.
projects.canonical_data: the connected working tree plus a local agent database of sessions, plans, memory, and diff history
projects.current_repo_note: The sweep proposed a workflow role describing a product that no longer exists: the browser toolbar was removed in November 2025 and the current product is a browser shipping its own agent. Its licence file is the canonical copyleft text with a seventeen-line addendum appended, carving out bundled icons the shipped application depends on as neither open source nor redistributable; neither the readme nor the platform's detection reflects that. The tree names two different legal entities for the same vendor.
strengths: The agent reads the live page, with the console and page structure supplied as environment adapters rather than screenshots pasted into a prompt

The approval default is centralised in one constant with a written rationale for why stored migrations must not reference it, so the safe default cannot drift between the backend, the interface, and the database
Unit tests are a required gate on two operating systems, followed by cross-platform packaging with a smoke test
weaknesses: The licence file appends a carve-out for bundled icons the shipped application depends on, which neither the readme nor automated detection reflects
The shipped default routes inference through the vendor's own proxy against an account token, so bringing your own key is the configured path rather than the out-of-box one
The product replaced its own toolbar with a browser less than a year ago, so the current boundary has little operating history, and the tree names two different legal entities
projects.why_it_matters: The only reviewed coding agent whose primary surface is a browser it ships itself, giving the agent the running page's console and structure as first-class context rather than as pasted evidence.

projects.name: grok-cli
projects.description: Terminal coding agent for one vendor's model API with subagent delegation, scheduled headless runs, host desktop automation, and remote control over a messaging bot.
projects.canonical_data: the working tree, a local session and transcript store, saved schedules and run logs, and a generated wallet file under the user's home directory
projects.current_repo_note: Distinct from the published community agent for the same model family on capabilities and canonical data rather than on interfaces, where it is the poorer of the two: it has no client-protocol surface, while the other does. Its licence is a template that was never filled in, naming no copyright holder. The last change to the default branch predates this review by three and a half months, and three pull requests claiming security fixes have been open since mid-2026.
strengths: Hooks block at tool-call time across eighteen lifecycle events with a documented exit-code contract, rather than asking the model to obey prose
Unattended operation is first-class, with a scheduling daemon keeping persisted run logs and a batch mode against the provider's own batch interface, both covered by tests
Release engineering is unusually careful for the size, with reproducible per-platform binaries carrying checksums and build-provenance attestations
weaknesses: The file tools resolve absolute paths without any workspace containment, and the change fixing it has been open since July 2026 alongside two other unmerged security fixes
Two hundred and forty-eight tests exist and no workflow runs them; continuous integration gates formatting, linting, typing, and a build only
The licence is a template with the copyright holder never filled in, and a generated wallet private key sits in plain text under the user's home directory
projects.why_it_matters: The most adopted independent coding agent built for one vendor's model API, and the only published one combining subagent delegation with scheduled unattended runs and host desktop automation.

projects.name: BeeAI Framework
projects.description: Python and TypeScript framework for building tool-using agents, with provider adapters, declarative tool-use requirements, and delegation and pipeline primitives for running several agents together.
projects.canonical_data: application-defined agent memory, workflow state, and serialised agent snapshots
projects.current_repo_note: The sweep read the orchestrator role from a readme headline promising multi-agent systems, which is the framing the curation rules say not to classify on. The coordination layer is under five per cent of the package against eleven thousand lines of provider adapters, so the roles are the inverse of two published orchestrators and were decided the same way. Its delegation and workflow primitives were confirmed present in the shipped package by running it offline against stub agents.
strengths: Its declarative requirement system is real control machinery rather than prompt guidance, validating rule sets at construction and raising on contradictions, with an approval gate that interposes before named tools run
Provider and protocol breadth without lock-in, covering many model providers plus local runtimes, three agent-serving protocols, and bridges into four other frameworks
The delegation and workflow primitives are implemented in the shipped package, confirmed by running it offline against stub agents
weaknesses: Its own headline promises multi-agent systems, but the coordination layer is a linear pipeline over a routing engine it never routes with, plus an agent-as-tool handoff
Two years and eighty-two releases in, it remains a pre-release version with no development-status classifier, and its flagship agent sits in an experimental package
The second language implementation is a lagging sibling rather than a peer, several releases and a month behind, with a fraction of the test tree
projects.why_it_matters: Shows what a vendor-neutral agent framework looks like when tool-use control is declarative and validated ahead of the run, and when one agent definition can be served over three interoperability protocols unchanged.

projects.name: Memobase
projects.description: Self-hosted memory server that turns chat transcripts into a configurable per-user profile and a searchable event timeline, and serves them over an API, three client libraries, and a tool server.
projects.canonical_data: a per-user profile organised by topic and an event timeline with embedded summaries, in a relational database with vector search, buffered through a cache; raw transcripts are discarded after processing unless retention is enabled
projects.current_repo_note: Development stopped in January 2026 with several unanswered contributions, and the maintaining organisation's readme now opens by promoting a separate project that makes no reference back to this one, so no successor is declared and the supersession rule does not apply. Every first-party hosted surface is unreachable: the homepage and cloud sign-in return not-found, the playground fails, and the documented cloud host does not resolve; only the documentation site answers. The self-hosted path is intact, which is why this is not the dormancy shape that holds other candidates. No published runtime names it as a backend; its integrations run one way from its own clients.
strengths: The memory unit is a configurable per-user profile with an event timeline rather than an undifferentiated fact pile, with worked schemas shipped so an operator decides what is worth remembering before extraction
Genuinely replaceable infrastructure: three client libraries, a broad API, a tool server, and a drop-in patch that adds memory to an existing model call, all against one self-hosted stack
Profiles and events are directly editable and deletable through the API, and raw transcripts are discarded after processing by default
